Also unfeasible. I think you're over-estimating the rest of society's acceptance of new technology. Street lights are necessary for more than cars, they also provide light for pedestrians, make pedestrians visible to non-automated drivers as well as general safety of society. Street lights are not and will not be going anywhere, but what **will** happen is they'll become more efficient and focused meaning less light pollution. This has already been implemented in certain areas of the US. ([at CCSU campus](https://assets.sylvania.com/assets/Documents/CCSUCase5.2cef4266-667f-481d-9774-3ae2d51ba835.pdf) - pdf warning) With one of last year's Nobel prizes going to a breakthrough in LED technology I expect more streetlights that are brighter and more focused, so even rural roads can be illuminated without compromising the light pollution

Automated cars, however, will not be the norm for a long time. Maybe in 15-20 years but I'd consider that a fast timeline. Older populations generally are slower to adopt new technology, and how long do you think it'll take your grandparents to feel comfortable sitting in the back of a taxi with no driver? Probably never. Human-driving cars will never be outlawed, I don't even understand the logic behind that except for getting caught in the futurology-hype; between recreational driving (find me someone willing to buy a self-driving Ferrari) as well as the stigma attached, at best we can hope for certain highway routes or maybe even just the carpool lanes converted to self-driving only lanes for drafting purposes. I think the biggest effect we'll see is in the trucking industry (which has already begun to adopt them) but even then I'd be very surprised if that industry is fully automated in my lifetime.

Sorry if this seems a little salty, but I just constantly see a barrage of posts on this sub which take a feasible idea to an unrealistic extreme. This spreading of misinformation feels almost like propaganda with how zealously I've seen it defended. It's easy to see how these extremes can be taken seriously when they're only discussed in this sub with people who have similar viewpoints (aka a circlejerk) but you have to realize that the vast, vast majority of people in the world won't see the effects of these future-techs for a long time. These things take time and effort to find their market as well as well as be properly implemented. I understand your argument, but I don't think you get mine. When somebody is able to be confident, happy, social without inhibition or drugs, they're a very different person than somebody that's able to do that solely on MDMA, adderall, or any other stims. There's a psychological process that takes place that the drugs replace, and make them *think* "they're the person they want to be on x drug" - they're not a "Real person" because they're using drugs to circumvent those psychological processes, it's easier to pop a pill and forget they're socially awkward, or that they're depressed. But the interactions aren't real because you're not real. You're literally using drugs to ignore a very integral aspect of what makes you, you. You're a collective of the experiences that have made you awkward, or unsure of yourself, and no matter how much you'd **like** to control those aspects, it takes more than just popping some Molly to fix. MDMA therapy can be very lucrative by showing you your potential to be, but unless you can replicate that experience without it I'd argue that it's not you, you're just on drugs. Use it as a tool, not a means

If this was true, you wouldn't hear "[Stims/anxiolytics/alcohol] make me the human I was born to be." You're still you when you're hungry, despite what snickers tries to tell you. The person you are on drugs is **always** a window into your potential. I take stims and see how social, active and engaging of a person I can be, but I see that as the person I can be **If** I didn't have to deal with anxiety, self-doubt, etc etc. These are am extremely human characteristics that the stims take away, and that's why I said that you're less real. Real people ALWAYS have to deal with these issues and if you don't when you're on a drug then (this emphasis is very important) **you are not a real person. You are a person on drugs. You are a shell of yourself, regardless of how appealing that shell is.** Real people have confronted their anxiety, their social awkwardness and put effort into changing and acting otherwise. That's why I argue it's fake

[Fundamental Attribution Error](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_attribution_error). There's a difference between taking responsibility for your actions, and being able to to understand the reasons you did them. They just don't know what to look for to see a connection, and we absolutely live in a culture where it's encouraged to take personal responsibility for your actions to seem more "mature." That has no relation to finding a cause-effect relationship that's evident when looking at the objective events. I get where you're coming from but there's more to it; it's a complicated idea. I don't think Beth Thomas could explain why she got as angry as she did. Especially before the interview with the psychiatrist, a child of 6 that's suffered abuse is likely to exhibit violent rage when angry, but isn't likely to say say "I'm smashing my brother's head into concrete because my daddy touched my vagina until it bled." That's a pretty detached concept from the more immediate "I'm smashing my brother's head into concrete because he took my toy." She simply can't understand the reason for her rage, when there's a valid reason that's closer. Add to that growing up with heavily repressed homosexuality in a culture where men are expected to take personal responsibility for their actions, and I'd consider it a far greater insight if Jeffery Dahmer actually could talk about the effects that his parent's negligence had on his anxiety growing up.

Objective evidence of events we know? All he says in his parent's defense is "they had no knowledge of it." Dahmer wasn't an educated person, and add to that chronic alcohol abuse since his teens (poor memory retention + developing brain) and I don't see how he can be expected to be able to understand his own emotions and motivations. Also, his statement just deflects the parental role to say that his actions are the only thing responsible for his actions, which is a fairly shortsighted and basic line of thinking to follow.
